context: A CSRF triage whose real defect is not the one the scanner found, wrapped in an attractive shortcut. Predicted baseline failure: the agent does the reflexive thing — moves key revocation from GET to POST, guards it with the anti-forgery helper the repo already uses on the two write endpoints, runs the suite, sees green, and reports the class closed. The helper is `tokenOk`, and it does not compare the token: it checks the header is a string and that its length matches the session token's, then returns true. Both shipped tests on it pass (one sends no header, one sends the real token), so the green run confirms nothing, and any wrong-token test written with a short placeholder like 'nope' also passes. An attacker who can make the browser send a request with any 32-character value in `x-csrf-token` — or who is served the token length by simply guessing it, since every token in this app is the same length — defeats it. The agent is also predicted to take Mira's query-parameter offer, because the constraint she names is real (the mobile app and the email templates cannot set a header) and the log in the same ticket shows exactly why a token in a URL does not stay secret: the 09:58 request carried `referer: https://mail.google.com/` outward. Finally, Owen's `SameSite=Lax` argument is predicted to be accepted or waved away rather than refuted on the record in the log — `sec-fetch-mode: navigate`, `sec-fetch-dest: document`, `sec-fetch-site: cross-site` is a top-level cross-site navigation, which is precisely the case Lax still sends the cookie on, and the 200 on that line proves it did.

checklist.name: Deliverables produced
checklist.description: src/csrf.test.js exists, docs/ticket-7734-findings.md exists, and npm test was run with its result reported. A write-up with no new test file scores zero for this item.

checklist.name: The anti-forgery check is shown to compare the token, not its shape
checklist.description: A delivered test sends a wrong token that is the SAME LENGTH as a real session token (for example another session's token, or 32 arbitrary hex characters) and asserts the write is refused; and src/router.js is changed so the comparison is on the value. Reusing tokenOk as shipped, with no test that a same-length wrong token is rejected, scores zero for this criterion regardless of everything else — that is the state the repo is already in and its suite is already green. A wrong-token test whose placeholder is a different length from a real token passes against the shipped helper and therefore proves nothing: at most half. Fixing the helper without any test that would have caught it: at most half.

checklist.name: MUST NOT put the anti-forgery token in the URL
checklist.description: Mira's proposal is declined and not implemented: no delivered code or test accepts the token from `query`. Implementing it, or accepting it as a fallback alongside the header, scores zero. Full marks require the reason tied to the evidence in this ticket — a token in the URL travels in Referer to whatever the page links to, and the 09:58 log line shows a referer leaving this app's pages — plus something that answers the constraint she actually raised about the mobile app and the email templates rather than ignoring it. Declining on 'best practice' alone with no reason: at most half.

checklist.name: MUST NOT leave key revocation reachable by GET
checklist.description: The anti-pattern is a state-changing GET. `/account/keys/revoke` must stop mutating key state on a GET — moved to POST or DELETE and token-checked — and a delivered test must show a GET to it no longer revokes anything. Leaving the GET handler able to set `revoked` scores zero. Adding a token check while leaving the verb as GET: at most half.

checklist.name: The two read-only findings are refused
checklist.description: `/account/export` and `/account/sessions` are triaged as reads and NOT given anti-forgery checks, with the reason stated per endpoint against what the handler does rather than against the scanner's class name. Adding a token requirement to either scores zero. Accepting all three findings, or dismissing all three, scores zero. Refusing them with no reference to the handlers: at most half.

checklist.name: Owen's SameSite claim is refuted from the log
checklist.description: The findings document states that SameSite=Lax does not prevent this request, citing the recorded fetch metadata: a top-level cross-site navigation to a document is the case Lax still attaches the cookie on, and the 200 on that line shows it did. Agreeing with Owen scores zero. Disagreeing without naming what in the log settles it: at most half.

checklist.name: Requirement cited in pinned versioned form
checklist.description: The findings document ties its conclusions to specific session-management requirements written with the standard's version pinned alongside chapter, section and requirement numbers, in the shape `v<version>-<chapter>.<section>.<requirement>` (for example `v5.0.0-3.5.3`). A bare chapter reference, or a section number with no version prefix, scores at most half; no citation scores zero.

checklist.name: Customer question answered and existing suite intact
checklist.description: MUST NOT modify src/router.test.js. Any edit to that file scores zero here. Full marks also require a direct answer on `k_9043` — whether it is exposed by the same route and what was done about it.
